references.anchor: ## 4.4 — Context Windows: The System's Working Memory
references.copy: > 📼 **Rewind it:** Cher's closet computer was useful because it had the available clothes, the occasion, and the choice in front of it. references.anchor: ## 5.2 — The Core Idea: Guess, Check, Adjust
references.copy: > 📼 **Rewind it:** If you remember recording an answering-machine greeting, listening back, hating one word, and doing another take, the shape is familiar: attempt, compare, adjust, repeat. Training does this with maths and enormous amounts of data — not taste, embarrassment, or self-awareness.
references.teachingJob: Turns the optimisation loop into a visible repeated action.
references.limitation: A model does not hear itself, dislike an attempt, or understand the correction.

references.anchor: ### Pipeline 1: Transcribe → Think → Speak Back (the chain)
references.copy: > 📼 **Rewind it:** This chain can feel like a late-'90s phone tree: one specialist takes the message, passes it on, and another delivers the reply. Each handoff can lose tone or detail before the next step begins. A native voice model shortens that chain; it does not become human or understand you the way a person does.
references.teachingJob: Explains why multi-model voice pipelines can introduce delay and information loss.
references.limitation: Not every handoff loses information, and native audio is not proof of human understanding.

references.anchor: ## 7.3 — Why the Same Prompt Gives Different Answers
references.copy: > 📼 **Rewind it:** Turning temperature down is a Miranda Priestly edit pass: fewer next-word options are allowed onto the runway, so the result is usually more consistent. That does not make it more intelligent, more factual, or automatically correct.

references.limitation: Stored preferences are not automatically harmful; distinguish product storage and retrieval from model weights and current context.

clarifications.anchor: > 📌 **The Four Layers — Complete Picture**
clarifications.copy: > ⏸️ **One distinction before the shorthand:** Machine learning, deep learning, and modern generative AI can be pictured as a model family. Agentic AI is different: it is the wider system around a model — a loop that can plan, take a step, inspect what happened and adjust, sometimes using memory, tools or a check with you. It is not simply a fourth, smarter model nested inside the other three.

clarifications.anchor: **What's the risk? (Model collapse)**
clarifications.copy: One technical distinction matters before we get to the risk: this does not usually mean one model is training itself. A model generates new examples, and those examples may then be selected or mixed into the data used to train another model. Synthetic data can be useful; the danger comes from how it is produced, checked, mixed, and reused over time.

clarifications.anchor: Ask an AI "how many r's are in the word strawberry?" and it will confidently tell you two. The answer is three. Try it yourself — this isn't a rare glitch. As of 2026, even frontier models get this wrong more often than they get it right.
clarifications.copy: Ask an AI how many r's are in "strawberry" and it may answer correctly — but letter-counting has historically been an unexpectedly awkward task for language models. The answer is three. The interesting question is why a system that handles complex language can still stumble over a simple-looking spelling task.

clarifications.anchor: The answer is in how the machine reads — or rather, how it *doesn't* read. Because a machine can't read English. It can't read any language. It doesn't see words, and it definitely doesn't see individual letters. What it works with is numbers — sequences of numbers. Every piece of maths inside the system operates on numbers, and your text has to become numbers before anything can happen.
clarifications.copy: The answer is in what reaches the model. It does not receive a page the way your eyes do. A tokeniser first divides the text into reusable pieces and maps those pieces to numbers. A piece can be a whole word, part of one, punctuation or even a single character, depending on the language, model and encoding. The model then works with that numbered sequence.

clarifications.anchor: And that strawberry question? The model never sees the individual letters. It sees `straw` + `berry` (or similar chunks) — and from those chunks, it has no way to inspect which letters appear inside. That's not a bug in its intelligence. It's a direct consequence of how this chopping works. Let's look at it.
clarifications.copy: And that strawberry question? The model usually processes one or more token pieces rather than starting with a neat row of letters. Some tokens may contain several characters; others may contain only one. That makes character-by-character work less direct than ordinary language prediction, although modern systems can sometimes compensate through learned patterns, reasoning or tools. Let's look at the chopping process.

clarifications.anchor: **Step 1:** Start with individual characters. Every letter, number, and punctuation mark is a token: `a`, `b`, `c`, ... `z`, `0`, `1`, ... `9`, `.`, `,`, `!`, etc.
clarifications.copy: **Step 1:** Begin with small base units. In this simplified character-level BPE example, those units are individual characters such as `a`, `b`, `1`, `.` and `!`. Real tokenisers vary: some start from bytes, characters, words or other pre-tokenised pieces.

clarifications.anchor: This process is called **Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)**, and it's what most major language models use — GPT, Claude, and others all build their vocabularies this way.
clarifications.copy: This simplified merge process describes **Byte Pair Encoding (BPE),** one widely used family of subword tokenisation methods. Other tokenisers use different starting units or algorithms, so the exact vocabulary and split depend on the model and encoding.

clarifications.anchor: The result: common English words are typically one token each. Less common words split into 2-3 pieces. Very rare words might split into many small pieces. And the system can handle anything — even nonsense text or a language it barely knows — by falling back to smaller and smaller chunks.
clarifications.copy: The result in a typical English-focused subword tokeniser: many common words use one token, while less common or unusual text may need several smaller pieces. Exact splits vary by language, model and encoding, so English rules of thumb do not travel unchanged.

clarifications.anchor: > 🔍 **Concept in Practice: Why AI can't count the r's in "strawberry"** You may have seen this: ask an AI "how many r's are in strawberry?" and it confidently answers "2." The answer is 3. Why does it get this wrong? Because the model never sees individual letters. It sees *tokens* — and "strawberry" likely gets split into chunks like `str` + `aw` + `berry`. The system processes those chunks as units. It has no way to examine individual characters inside a token, the same way you can't easily count the number of times a specific thread appears in a woven fabric just by looking at the overall pattern. That's tokenisation in action: the model is extraordinarily good at language — grammar, meaning, reasoning, style — because it operates at the chunk level. But tasks that require character-level inspection (counting specific letters, reversing words letter by letter, checking spelling character by character) are structurally hard for it. Not a bug in the intelligence — a direct consequence of how the input gets chopped up before the model ever sees it.
clarifications.copy: > 🔍 **Concept in Practice: Why letter-counting can be harder than it looks** A model normally predicts from token pieces, not from a purpose-built letter counter. If "strawberry" arrives as several multi-character pieces, counting one particular letter requires an extra character-level step that ordinary next-token prediction does not directly provide. That can make tasks such as counting letters, reversing a word or checking a spelling less reliable than their simplicity suggests. It is a tendency, not a permanent inability: a model may answer correctly from learned examples, deliberate reasoning or a tool. The useful lesson is to check exact-character tasks rather than assuming language fluency guarantees them.

clarifications.anchor: **Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)** — The most common method for building a token vocabulary. Starts from individual characters, repeatedly merges the most common adjacent pairs until the vocabulary reaches its target size.
clarifications.copy: **Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)** — A widely used method for building a subword vocabulary by repeatedly merging frequent adjacent pieces. This chapter uses a simplified character-level example; real tokenisers may begin from bytes or other units.

clarifications.anchor: **This is why you see responses appear word by word in a chat interface** — each word appears as it's generated. The model isn't writing the whole response and then showing it to you. It's producing it live, token by token.
clarifications.copy: **This is why you see responses appear piece by piece in a chat interface.** The model is not writing the whole response and then revealing it. It generates one token at a time, and the interface updates as tokens arrive. A token may be a whole word, part of one, punctuation or another reusable piece, so the visible updates do not map neatly to one word each.

clarifications.anchor: > 🔍 **Concept in Practice: Why responses stream in word by word** When you watch an AI response appear gradually — word by word, sometimes pausing mid-sentence — you're watching the decode phase in real time. Each word you see appear is a newly generated token. The pauses happen when the model is computing the probability distribution for the next token. It's not "thinking" in a human sense — it's running the maths for the next prediction.
clarifications.copy: > 🔍 **Concept in Practice: Why responses stream piece by piece** When an AI response appears gradually, you are watching the decode phase reach the interface. The model selects one token, appends it, then repeats. The product may display one token immediately or batch several into a smoother update, so a visible word is not proof of one token. A pause can reflect next-token computation, tool use, network delay or interface batching; the animation is not a window into human-style thought.

clarifications.anchor: 6. **Streaming** — each token is sent to your screen as it's generated (that's why responses appear word by word)
clarifications.copy: 6. **Streaming** — generated tokens are delivered toward the interface as they become available; the product may display them individually or in small batches, so the response appears piece by piece rather than in a guaranteed one-word-per-token rhythm

clarifications.anchor: **Watch the streaming.** Next time you use an AI chatbot, watch the response appear. Notice it comes word by word (or chunk by chunk). That's the decode phase in real time. Each word you see is a new token being generated.
clarifications.copy: **Watch the streaming.** Next time you use an AI chatbot, watch the response appear in pieces. That is the interface receiving live generated output, sometimes one token at a time and sometimes in small batches. The useful clue is that the answer is still being produced—not that each visible word equals one token.

clarifications.anchor: Everything the system can "see" during a single conversation has to fit inside this window: your message, the system's instructions, any documents you've attached, and the *entire conversation history* up to that point.
clarifications.copy: Everything the system can "see" for one request has to fit inside this window: your message, the system's instructions, any documents the product supplies, and whatever earlier conversation the product includes. A product may drop, summarise or omit older material, so the model does not necessarily receive a perfect copy of the whole chat.

clarifications.anchor: | Why conversations have limits | The entire conversation history lives inside the context window. When it fills up, old messages get dropped. |
clarifications.copy: | Why conversations have limits | The product has to fit the current request and whatever earlier material it supplies inside the context window. Older messages may be dropped, summarised or omitted. |

clarifications.anchor: Every time you send a new message, the *entire conversation history* — every message you've sent and every response it gave — gets loaded into the context window alongside your new message. The model reads the whole thing from scratch, every single turn. It's not recalling anything from memory. It's re-reading the transcript.
clarifications.copy: Every time you send a new message, the product assembles a new context for that request. It may include your new message, system instructions and some earlier conversation, but it can drop, summarise or omit older material. The model works from whatever the product supplies on that turn; it is not privately recalling the whole transcript from its own memory.

clarifications.anchor: 6. **Response delivered.** You get an accurate answer about *your company's specific policy* — even though the model was never trained on your HR documents.
clarifications.copy: 6. **Response delivered.** You get an answer grounded in the policy text the system retrieved — even though the model was never trained on your HR documents. You still need to check that it retrieved the right, current passages and represented them correctly.

clarifications.anchor: > 💡 **Training vs RAG — two ways to give a model information** **Training:** Bake information permanently into the weights. Expensive, slow, frozen once done. Good for general knowledge and capabilities. **RAG:** Retrieve information on-the-fly and inject into context. Cheap, fast, always current. Good for specific, private, or frequently-changing information. Most production AI systems use both: a pre-trained model (general knowledge in weights) + RAG (specific current knowledge retrieved into context). Neither alone is sufficient.
clarifications.copy: > 💡 **Training vs RAG — two ways to give a model information** **Training:** Bake patterns into the weights. Expensive, slow and frozen once done. Good for general knowledge and capabilities. **RAG:** Retrieve selected information at answer time and inject it into context. It can use newer, specific or private material without retraining — but only if the source collection is current and the system retrieves the right passages. Most production AI systems use both: a pre-trained model plus retrieval for information needed now. Neither route guarantees a correct answer.

clarifications.anchor: **When it's not enough:** When you need the model to consistently behave in a very specific way (always use a particular format, always adopt a particular tone) across thousands of interactions without repeating the examples every time. Prompts live in the context window — they have to be sent every single time. If your behaviour modification takes 500 tokens of examples and instructions, you're paying for those 500 tokens on every single request, forever. That's when you consider baking the behaviour in permanently through fine-tuning.
clarifications.copy: **When it's not enough:** When you need a model version to make a particular format or tone more likely across many interactions without sending the same examples every time. Prompts and examples are supplied in the context for each request. If those instructions are long and repeated at scale, fine-tuning may be worth testing — but changing the weights does not guarantee that the model will follow the pattern every time.

clarifications.anchor: **What RAG changes:** What the model *knows about.* It gives the model access to specific, current, or private information it was never trained on.
clarifications.copy: **What RAG changes:** What information the model can use for this request. It can give the model access to selected specific, newer or private information that was not stored in its trained weights. The answer still depends on the source collection, retrieval and generation all working well.

clarifications.anchor: **Fine-tuning** changes the approach entirely. Instead of instructing the model to behave differently, you actually **change its weights** — retrain it on thousands of examples of the exact behaviour you want. After fine-tuning, the SOAP format isn't something the model is being *told* to do. It's something the model *does naturally*, because its weights have been adjusted to make that format the default.
clarifications.copy: **Fine-tuning** changes the model version itself. Instead of supplying the same instruction only in the current request, you train on examples of the behaviour you want and adjust the model's weights before later use. That can make SOAP-format responses more likely without repeating the full example set each time. It does not make the format automatic: the fine-tuned model still needs testing on real and unfamiliar cases.

clarifications.anchor: - You need the model to adopt a domain-specific tone or vocabulary permanently — not "when reminded" but as its natural voice
clarifications.copy: - You need a model version to favour a domain-specific tone or vocabulary across many requests, and prompting alone is not reliable enough

clarifications.anchor: **The result:** A model that's been shaped by human preferences to be helpful, follow instructions, refuse harmful requests, and produce quality outputs. Every major chatbot you've used (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini) has been through this process.
clarifications.copy: **The result:** A model version whose responses have been shaped toward preferences such as helpfulness, instruction-following and safer refusal behaviour. Those are tendencies, not guarantees, and providers can use different combinations of preference-training methods.

clarifications.anchor: **DPO (Direct Preference Optimisation):** A shortcut. Instead of building a separate reward model first, DPO skips that step and directly adjusts the main model based on the preference pairs. "Humans preferred Response A over Response B — adjust the weights to produce more A-like responses." Same outcome, fewer steps. It's like cutting out the middleman — instead of training a judge and then training the employee based on the judge's scores, you just show the employee directly which work was preferred and let them learn from that.
clarifications.copy: **DPO (Direct Preference Optimisation):** A more direct preference-training method. Instead of first training a separate reward model and then using reinforcement learning, DPO adjusts the model from pairs such as "humans preferred Response A over Response B." It pursues a similar broad aim with a different training procedure; it does not promise an identical model or identical results.

clarifications.anchor:
| Its consistent behaviour pattern (format, style, tone) | **Fine-tuning** | Bakes behaviour into the weights permanently |
| Its safety and helpfulness characteristics | **RLHF / DPO** | Shapes deep behavioural tendencies through preference data |
clarifications.copy:
| Its recurring behaviour pattern (format, style, tone) | **Fine-tuning** | Adjusts the model version's weights so the pattern is more likely across later requests |
| Its safety and helpfulness tendencies | **RLHF / DPO** | Uses preference data to shape later behaviour, which still requires testing |

clarifications.anchor: **What RAG doesn't change:** How the model *behaves.* It still responds in the same style, follows the same patterns, has the same tendencies. It just has more (and better) information to work with.
clarifications.copy: **What RAG doesn't change:** The trained weights of the model version. Retrieved material can influence the answer, wording and format for this request, but RAG alone does not create a newly trained model version.

clarifications.anchor: **The practical test:** If your problem is "the model doesn't know the right answer" — RAG. If your problem is "the model knows the right answer but won't format it correctly or tone it the way we need" — that's a behaviour problem, and RAG won't help. You need fine-tuning.
clarifications.copy: **The practical test:** If the request needs information the model was not trained on, investigate retrieval. If the same format or tone keeps failing after good instructions and examples, test whether fine-tuning improves that recurring tendency. Many products use both, and neither should be chosen without evaluation.

clarifications.anchor: The difference: prompting is like telling someone "please speak French" every time (they can, but they have to think about it and sometimes slip). Fine-tuning is like the person living in France for a year until French becomes their default.
clarifications.copy: A rough analogy: prompting is like bringing a phrase card for this conversation; fine-tuning is more like practising the language before later conversations. Practice can make a response pattern more likely, but the person can still slip — and a model can too.

clarifications.anchor: - You want faster inference (because the behaviour is baked in, you don't need long prompts explaining what to do every time — which also saves money on input tokens)
clarifications.copy: - Repeated instructions are making every request long, and testing shows a fine-tuned model can meet the task with shorter inputs; measure the actual speed, quality and cost rather than assuming a saving

clarifications.anchor: 3. Fine-tune only if behaviour needs permanent change (weeks, $$)
clarifications.copy: 3. Test fine-tuning only when you need a stronger recurring behaviour tendency and prompting is not reliable enough

clarifications.anchor: The model does the generation. Everything else shapes what it generates, ensures it's safe, connects it to the outside world, and delivers it to you.
clarifications.copy: The model does the generation. The product around it decides what instructions and information to supply, may connect approved tools, may check the input or output, and delivers the result to you. Those layers can reduce risks; they do not ensure that every answer is safe or correct.

clarifications.anchor: Every AI product you use has all of these layers. The differences between products (why ChatGPT feels different from Claude, which feels different from Gemini) are mostly in the *layers around the model* — the system prompt, the tool access, the guardrails, the memory design — not just the model itself.
clarifications.copy: AI products use different combinations of these layers. A simple feature may wrap one model call; a larger product may add retrieval, memory, tools, routing and several checks. Products can feel different because of both the underlying model and the system built around it.

clarifications.anchor: The retailer pays per request — billed per token (input + output), the pricing from Chapter 4. For every customer interaction, a few cents goes to the API provider. The retailer gets AI capabilities without building or hosting anything.
clarifications.copy: The retailer pays the provider under that API's current pricing rules. Many text-model APIs charge for input and output tokens, but providers, models, tools, caching and media can change the bill. The retailer gets model access without training and operating that model itself, while still building and running the surrounding product.

clarifications.anchor: The model processes ALL of this as one combined input. It doesn't know which parts are "system instructions" vs "user message" vs "retrieved document" — it's all just tokens in a sequence. The harness assembled all five pieces in the right order. The model generates a response attending to all of them simultaneously.
clarifications.copy: The model processes the supplied material as one context sequence, but the product can preserve roles and boundaries using message roles, ordering, labels or other structure. The harness chooses what to include and how to arrange it. The model then generates from that supplied context; important material can still be omitted, misunderstood or outweighed by other content.

clarifications.anchor: **This is the harness's entire job: assembling the right context window, in the right order, with the right information, before the model ever runs.** The quality of the response is largely determined by what's in this window — not by the model's raw intelligence.
clarifications.copy: **Context assembly is one major harness job:** selecting and arranging the material supplied before the model runs. A harness may also manage tools, state, retries, checks and multi-step control. The response depends on both the model and the system around it—including whether the right information was selected.

clarifications.anchor: Real system prompts for production AI products are much longer — often 2,000-5,000 words. They include personality rules, formatting instructions, safety guidelines, tool documentation, and behavioural edge cases. Every word goes into your context window and uses tokens — that's why system prompts represent a real engineering trade-off: more detailed instructions = more predictable behaviour but less room for your actual conversation.
clarifications.copy: Production system instructions range from short to very long. They can include role, format, policy, tool and edge-case guidance. Supplied instructions use context space and input processing, but adding more words does not automatically make behaviour more predictable; teams test whether each instruction helps, conflicts or gets ignored.

clarifications.anchor: > ⏸️ **"But how does the system DECIDE it needs to search the web? Who makes that call?"** The model itself makes the decision — but only because the system prompt tells it it can. Here's what happens mechanically: The system prompt includes something like: "You have access to a web search tool. If the user asks about current events or information you're not confident about, call the tool." When the model generates its response, instead of producing regular text tokens, it can produce a special structured output that means "I want to call a tool." Something like: `{"tool": "web_search", "query": "latest iPhone price 2026"}` The orchestration layer sees this, pauses generation, runs the web search, gets results back, injects those results into the context window, and then tells the model: "OK, here are the search results. Now continue your response." The model then generates its actual answer using both the question and the fresh search results. So it's a collaboration: the model decides WHEN to use a tool (because it was trained to recognise when it needs external information). The orchestration layer handles the HOW (actually running the tool and managing the back-and-forth). Neither could do this alone.
clarifications.copy: > ⏸️ **"But how does the system decide it needs to search the web?"** A product can let the model propose a tool call, use separate routing rules, or combine both. In the model-proposal pattern, the supplied instructions describe an available tool and the model generates structured text naming that tool and proposed arguments. The orchestration layer—not the model alone—validates the request, decides whether it is allowed, runs the tool if approved, and adds the result to a later context. The model can then generate another step or an answer from that result.

clarifications.anchor: Modern AI products are orchestrated systems, not single model calls. The more capable the product seems, the more orchestration is happening behind the scenes.
clarifications.copy: Many AI products use orchestration when one model call is not enough. Others remain deliberately simple. Visible capability does not tell you how many hidden steps ran, so the useful question is which components the product actually called for this task.

clarifications.anchor: **Why this matters economically:** If every request went to the frontier model, costs would be unsustainable at scale. A product handling 10 million requests per day saves 70–90% on inference costs by routing appropriately — while users experience no quality difference on the easy requests.
clarifications.copy: **Why this matters economically:** routing can reduce cost and delay when a smaller or specialised model handles a task well enough. The saving and quality effect depend on the request mix, model prices, router errors and evaluation results; a cheaper route is not useful if it sends an important request to a model that cannot do the job.

clarifications.anchor:
When you open Claude and type a question, here's what actually happens:

1. **Wrapper** receives your message (the chat interface)
2. **Input guardrails** scan your message for policy violations
3. **Harness** assembles the context window:- Loads the system prompt

- Retrieves relevant memory facts about you
- Includes the conversation history
- Determines if tools are needed
- Injects the current date/time

1. **Router** picks the appropriate model (if the product uses routing)
2. **Model** runs inference (prefill → decode → generates tokens)
3. **Output guardrails** check the response before delivery
4. **Wrapper** streams the response to your screen

All of that happens in 1–5 seconds. Seven layers deep, multiple systems coordinating — and you just see words appearing in a chat box.
clarifications.copy:
When you type a question into an AI product, a typical route looks like this:

1. The **wrapper** receives your message.
2. The product may run an **input check**.
3. The **harness** assembles the context the model will receive: your message, system instructions and any relevant chat, retrieved documents, memory, date or tool result the product chooses to supply.
4. An optional **router** may select a model.
5. The selected **model** runs inference and generates tokens.
6. The product may run an **output check**.
7. The **wrapper** displays or streams the answer.

The exact layers and timing vary by product and request. The important separation is stable: the surrounding product builds and delivers the interaction; the model generates within what that product supplies.

clarifications.anchor: **API** — How applications send prompts to models and receive responses. Billed per token.
clarifications.copy: **API** — A defined way for one software system to send a request to another and receive a response. Many model APIs charge for input and output tokens, but pricing depends on the provider and service.

clarifications.anchor: **Router** — Chooses which model handles each request. Sends simple tasks to cheap models, complex tasks to powerful ones. Saves 70-90% on inference costs.
clarifications.copy: **Router** — Chooses which model or path handles a request. It can reduce cost or delay, but the result depends on how accurately it matches each task to a capable route.

clarifications.anchor:
```
                              ┌─── THE FULL PRODUCT STACK ───┐
                              │                              │
YOU → [Wrapper/UI] → [Input Guardrails] → [Harness/Orchestration] → [Router]
                                                    │                    ↓
                                          ┌─────────┼──────────┐   [Model Selection]
                                          │         │          │        ↓
                                     [Memory]  [RAG/Docs]  [Tools]  [MODEL]
                                          │         │          │        ↓
                                          └─────────┼──────────┘   [Generation]
                                                    │                    ↓
                                          [Output Guardrails] ← ─ ─ ─ ─ ┘
                                                    ↓
                                             [Response to YOU]

```
clarifications.copy:
```
YOU
 ↓
[Wrapper receives the message]
 ↓
[Optional input check]
 ↓
[Harness assembles the current context]
 ├── system instructions
 ├── relevant chat or memory
 ├── retrieved documents
 └── optional date or tool result
 ↓
[MODEL generates]
 ↑
 └ - - [Optional router may select a model] - -┘
 ↓
[Optional output check]
 ↓
[Wrapper shows the response]

```

clarifications.anchor: **Guardrails** | Filters and rules that check the model's output before it reaches you — blocking harmful, off-topic, or policy-violating content
clarifications.copy: **Guardrails** | Product checks or rules that may inspect an input, a proposed action or an output. They can reduce particular risks, but they do not make every result safe, correct or appropriate.

clarifications.anchor: **Think about routing.** If you use a product that offers model selection (like choosing between "fast" and "powerful" modes) — that's a router you're controlling manually. Products that don't show you this choice are still routing — just doing it automatically.
clarifications.copy: **Think about routing.** If a product lets you choose between model or mode options, you are making a visible routing choice. If it offers no choice, you cannot tell from the interface alone whether it routed the request automatically or simply used one model. Look for the product's own current documentation before claiming what happened behind the screen.

clarifications.anchor: **Orchestration** — Coordinating multiple steps, tools, or model calls in sequence. Most real AI products are orchestrated multi-step systems.
clarifications.copy: **Orchestration** — Coordinating multiple steps, tools or model calls. Some products use it for multi-step work; other features deliberately use one model call.

clarifications.anchor: **Guardrails** — Filters checking input and output for safety, policy compliance, and quality. Applied on both sides of the model.
clarifications.copy: **Guardrails** — Product checks or rules that may inspect an input, a proposed action or an output for a defined risk or policy. Their placement and coverage vary, and they do not guarantee a safe or correct result.

sprinkles.copy: Calling every useful computer feature AI? As if.
sprinkles.teachingJob: Lets the automation-versus-AI distinction land with a compact Clueless-era dismissal.
sprinkles.limitation: The mechanism is fully explained first; the phrase adds memory and voice rather than evidence.

sprinkles.anchor: Everything the system can "see" for one request has to fit inside this window: your message, the system's instructions, any documents the product supplies, and whatever earlier conversation the product includes. A product may drop, summarise or omit older material, so the model does not necessarily receive a perfect copy of the whole chat.
sprinkles.copy: In this case, *Mean Girls* got it backwards: "The limit does not exist." Here, it does.
sprinkles.teachingJob: Makes the finite context-window boundary memorable after the boundary has been defined.
sprinkles.limitation: The joke does not substitute for the following explanation of why the limit exists.

sprinkles.anchor: After billions of these rounds — billions of guesses, billions of tiny adjustments — the system has tuned its internal numbers to be very good at predicting what comes next in text. Not because anyone told it the rules of English. Because it saw so many examples that it absorbed the patterns: grammar, facts, style, reasoning, everything that shows up in the statistical structure of language.
sprinkles.copy: The unofficial training anthem is *Oops!... I Did It Again* — except every oops comes with a number showing how wrong the guess was.
sprinkles.teachingJob: Reinforces the repeated guess-measure-adjust loop after loss has been explained.
sprinkles.limitation: A model does not hear the song, feel regret, or understand its mistake.

sprinkles.anchor: The model hasn't forgotten — it never knew in the first place.
sprinkles.copy: New chat, new context: "We were on a break!"
sprinkles.teachingJob: Makes the separation between two chat contexts memorable.
sprinkles.limitation: The surrounding prose retains the product-memory exception and explains what can explicitly move between chats.
